procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 24.01.2023 of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in WPCRL No.596 of 2022
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the Writ Petition (WPCRL No. 596 of 2022) filed by the appellant (detenue's sister-in-law) challenging the detention order and its confirmation. The writ petition argued that relevant documents were not supplied to the detenue, and sought the detenue's release. A coordinate bench of the same High Court had previously allowed writ petitions filed by co-accused persons challenging the same detention order, holding that the non-supply of documents invalidated the detention order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed her writ petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, finding that the High Court should have followed the precedent set by the coordinate bench or referred the matter to a larger bench if it disagreed with the earlier decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal on the grounds that the High Court failed to follow the view taken by another Division Bench of the same High Court when the grounds of detention and challenge were identical.

directions: Order of detention dated 24th August 2021 passed by the Central Economic Intelligence Bureau, COFEPOSA Wing is quashed and set aside.
Order of confirmation of detention order dated 24th May 2022 passed by the Central Economic Intelligence Bureau, COFEPOSA Wing is quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Division Bench of a High Court is bound to follow the decision of a coordinate Bench of the same High Court when the grounds of detention and challenge are identical, and if it disagrees, what is the appropriate course of action?

facts: Multiple co-accused individuals were detained under the same order based on identical grounds and materials.

One Division Bench of the High Court heard the cases of some of the co-accused and quashed their detention orders. It found that the failure to supply requested documents (like WhatsApp chats) violated the detenus' right to make an effective representation.
Subsequently, a different Division Bench of the same High Court heard the case of another detenu from the same incident.

This second Bench, despite the identical grounds and challenge, disagreed with the first Bench's conclusion and upheld the detention order. It attempted to distinguish the prior ruling by stating the detaining authority had considered other materials as well.
law: The Supreme Court established the principle of judicial discipline, which dictates that a Division Bench of a High Court is bound by the decision of another coordinate Bench (a bench with the same number of judges) of the same court.
This principle is especially strong when the facts, grounds of detention, and legal challenges are identical in both cases.
If a coordinate Bench disagrees with an earlier decision by another coordinate Bench, it cannot simply ignore or overrule it.
The only proper course of action for the disagreeing Bench is to refer the matter to a larger Bench for an authoritative ruling.
application: The Supreme Court found that the second Division Bench should have followed the decision of the first coordinate Bench, as the cases were identical.

The Court rejected the second Bench's attempt to distinguish the earlier case. It noted that the "other material" the second Bench referred to was also present in the cases of the co-accused who were released by the first Bench, so it was not a valid point of distinction.
By ignoring the prior, binding decision and creating a conflicting judgment, the second Division Bench acted improperly and violated judicial discipline.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a Division Bench of a High Court must follow the decision of a coordinate Bench on an identical issue. If it believes the earlier decision is incorrect, its only option is to refer the matter to a larger Bench. The second Division Bench failed to do this, so its judgment was quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-supply of documents relied upon in a detention order, when requested by the detenue, vitiates the order by affecting the right to make an effective representation?

facts: A detention order was issued against a detenue and several co-accused based on the same grounds and materials.
The co-accused successfully challenged their detention before a Division Bench of the High Court, which held that the non-supply of requested documents vitiated the detention order.

However, a different (coordinate) Division Bench of the same High Court dismissed a similar petition filed on behalf of the current detenue, who was challenging the detention on the exact same grounds.
law: Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, a person under detention has a fundamental right to be given the earliest opportunity to make an effective representation against the detention order.

This right to representation obligates the detaining authority to furnish the detenue with all the documents and materials that were relied upon to make the detention order, especially when requested.

The principle of judicial discipline requires that a bench of a court follow the decision of a coordinate bench on an identical issue. If the bench disagrees, it must refer the matter to a larger bench.
application: The Supreme Court noted that a coordinate bench of the High Court had already decided the exact same issue for the co-accused, finding that the non-supply of documents violated their right to make an effective representation.
The Court held that the second Division Bench was bound by judicial discipline to follow this earlier decision, as the grounds of detention and the materials relied upon were identical.
The second bench's attempt to distinguish the cases was rejected, as the circumstances were the same for all detenus.

By failing to provide the requested documents, the detaining authority impaired the detenue's constitutional right under Article 22(5), making it impossible for them to make a full and effective representation against their detention.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the non-supply of documents relied upon in the detention order, when requested by the detenue, fatally vitiates the order. This failure constitutes a violation of the detenue's fundamental right under Article 22(5) of the Constitution to make an effective representation. Consequently, the detention order was quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Division Bench of a High Court is bound to follow the decision of a coordinate Bench of the same High Court when the grounds of detention and challenge are identical, and if it disagrees, what is the appropriate course of action?
appellant_arguments: A Division Bench of a High Court cannot ignore a decision by a coordinate Bench of the same court when the grounds of detention and the material relied upon are identical.

When a coordinate Bench had already concluded that the non-supply of documents vitiated the detention for co-accused persons, a subsequent Bench hearing the appellant's case on the same facts should have followed that precedent.
If the subsequent Division Bench believed the earlier decision was incorrect, the only proper judicial course was to refer the matter to a larger Bench, not to simply disregard the prior ruling.
respondent_arguments: The findings of the coordinate Bench in the cases of the co-accused were not binding or applicable in the appellant's case.
The detaining authority had considered other materials to arrive at its subjective satisfaction, justifying a different outcome from the cases of the co-accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the non-supply of documents relied upon in a detention order, when requested by the detenue, vitiates the order by affecting the right to make an effective representation?
appellant_arguments: The non-supply of documents that were relied upon in the detention order, despite a specific request from the detenue, is an infraction of the right to make an effective representation.

Since the contents of the requested documents were relied upon by the detaining authority to form its conclusion, they ought to have been furnished to the detenue to allow for a meaningful challenge to the detention.
respondent_arguments: There was no duty to supply the documents requested by the detenue.

The non-supply of certain documents, like WhatsApp chats, does not vitiate the detention order because the detaining authority arrived at its subjective satisfaction based on various other documents and materials.

cases.case_name: Official Liquidator v. Dayanand and Others
cases.principle: For the principle that the judicial fraternity has a duty to abide by the Constitution, respect its ideals and institutions, and observe constitutional principles with rigour, which supports the doctrine of judicial discipline requiring a coordinate bench to either follow a prior decision or refer the matter to a larger bench.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a Division Bench of a High Court is presented with a case where the grounds of challenge are identical to a case already decided by a coordinate Bench of the same court, it must follow the earlier view. If the Bench believes the earlier decision is incorrect in law, its only option is to refer the matter to a larger Bench.
obiter: In our constitutional set-up every citizen is under a duty to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions. Those who have been entrusted with the task of administering the system and operating various constituents of the State and who take oath to act in accordance with the Constitution and uphold the same, have to set an example by exhibiting total commitment to the constitutional ideals.
The right to make a representation carries with it the obligation on the part of the detaining authority to furnish the materials on which the detention order was made.

If the grounds for detention are not sufficient to enable the detenue to make a representation, the detenue can ask for particulars, and an infringement of this right entitles the person to be released by the court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Division Bench of a High Court committed a serious error of judicial discipline by failing to follow a decision of a coordinate Bench where the grounds of detention and the material relied upon were identical. The subsequent Bench was bound by the prior ruling that non-supply of requested documents vitiated the detention order. If the Bench disagreed with the earlier decision, its only permissible course of action was to refer the matter to a larger Bench, not to disregard the precedent and arrive at a conflicting conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: A Division Bench of a High Court is bound to follow the view taken by a coordinate Bench of the same High Court when the grounds of detention and challenge are identical.
If a Division Bench believes a prior decision by a coordinate Bench is incorrect in law, the only available option is to refer the matter to a larger Bench.

Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, if the grounds supplied are insufficient for a detenue to make an effective representation, the detenue has a right to ask for particulars, and an infringement of this right necessitates the detenue's release.
policy_considerations: In our constitutional set-up, every citizen, and particularly members of the judicial fraternity, are under a duty to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, exhibiting total commitment to constitutional principles to maintain judicial propriety and consistency.
